label: The Founding Fathers
notes: This short historical chapter spans printed pages twenty-nine through thirty-eight. It traces one idea across two centuries: how to move mass from a source to a target as cheaply as possible. We meet Monge with his deterministic map, then Kantorovich with his relaxed plan, and finally the modern revival that fused the problem with analysis and geometry.

label: Monge 1781: Deblais et Remblais
notes: Begin in 1781 with Monge's memoir on cuttings and fillings. A pile of earth, the deblai, must be carted to fill a hole, the remblai, of equal volume. Every grain travels somewhere, and the engineer pays the total work. Monge fixed the cost equal to the distance carried and asked which assignment minimises that bill.

label: The Monge Problem
notes: Formalise Monge as a search over transport maps. A map sends each source point to one target point and must push the source measure forward onto the target. We minimise the integral of the cost of displacement. The constraint that a single point cannot be split is exactly what makes this minimisation delicate and sometimes unsolvable.

label: Transport Maps and Non-Splitting
notes: Stress the rigidity built into a map. Mass at a point is indivisible; it travels as one block to a single destination. Push-forward records that the target histogram is exactly the image of the source under T. When a single atom must supply two separated targets, no admissible map exists, foreshadowing why relaxation is needed.

label: Monge's Geometric Insight
notes: Monge reasoned geometrically as well as analytically. For the distance cost in the plane he argued the optimal transport rays are straight segments that never cross, since crossing paths could be uncrossed to save length. The rays cut orthogonally across a family of surfaces, an early glimpse of the geometry later formalised through potentials and gradients.

label: Why Maps Can Fail
notes: Here is the structural defect. The Monge problem optimises over maps, a set that is neither convex nor closed, so a minimising sequence can escape the admissible class. A Dirac source has no map to a spread target. Existence therefore requires extra regularity, and for over a century the problem stalled on exactly this point.

label: Kantorovich 1942: The Relaxation
notes: Kantorovich's 1942 move was to stop tracking where each grain lands and instead record how much mass flows between every pair of locations. This object is a transport plan, a coupling of the two measures. Maps become a special case where the plan concentrates on a graph, and the search now ranges over a far friendlier set.

label: The Kantorovich Problem
notes: State the relaxed problem precisely. We minimise the integral of the cost against a coupling whose two marginals are the prescribed source and target measures. The admissible couplings form a convex, weakly compact set, and the cost is linear, so a minimiser always exists. This is a tractable linear program over measures.

label: Monge versus Kantorovich
notes: Place the two formulations side by side. Monge searches deterministic maps over a non-convex set where solutions may not exist. Kantorovich searches couplings over a convex compact set where they always do, and the optimal cost never exceeds Monge's. Under mild conditions the optimal plan is induced by a map, reconciling the two.

label: Kantorovich Duality
notes: Relaxation unlocks duality. The minimal transport cost equals a maximisation over pairs of potentials whose sum is bounded by the cost. The potentials act as prices: a certificate that no cheaper plan exists. Kantorovich's linear programming insight earned him the 1975 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics for resource allocation.

label: The Modern Revival
notes: Trace the renaissance. Brenier identified optimal maps for quadratic cost with gradients of convex potentials, tying transport to the Monge-Ampere equation. McCann built displacement interpolation, Otto recast diffusion as gradient flow on Wasserstein space, and the field fused with fluid mechanics, partial differential equations, and Riemannian geometry.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by gathering the thread. One engineering question about moving earth became, through relaxation and duality, a bridge between probability, analysis, and geometry. Remember the hierarchy: Monge poses the rigid map, Kantorovich relaxes to plans and gains existence and duality, and the moderns supply the structure that makes the optimum computable and geometric.
